segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I must boast; there is nothing to be gained by it, but I will go on to visions and revelations of the Lord.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I know a man in Christ who fourteen years ago—whether in the body I do not know, or outside the body I do not know; God knows—was snatched away as far as the third heaven.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And I know that such a man—whether in the body or apart from the body I do not know; God knows—

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: was snatched away into paradise and heard unutterable words, which no human being is permitted to speak.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: On behalf of such a man I will boast, but on my own behalf I will not boast, except in my weaknesses.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For if I should want to boast, I will not be a fool, for I will be speaking the truth. But I refrain, so that no one will credit me with more than what they see in me or hear from me,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: even given the extraordinary character of the revelations. Therefore, so that I would not become conceited, a thorn in the flesh was given to me, a messenger of Satan to beat me, so that I would not become conceited.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Three times I pleaded with the Lord about this, that it would leave me.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he has said to me,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “My grace is enough for you, for power is brought to completion in weakness.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So I will most gladly boast in my weaknesses instead, so that the power of Christ may make its dwelling upon me.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: That is why I am content in weaknesses, in insults, in hardships, in persecutions and distresses, for Christ’s sake; for when I am weak, then I am powerful.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I have become a fool; you forced me to it. For I ought to have been commended by you, since I was in no way inferior to the super-apostles, even if I am nothing.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The signs of an apostle were indeed worked among you with all endurance, by signs and wonders and acts of power.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For in what way were you made worse off than the rest of the assemblies, except that I myself was not a burden to you? Forgive me this wrong!

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Look, I am ready to come to you this third time, and I will not be a burden; for I am not seeking what is yours, but you. For children ought not to save up for their parents, but parents for their children.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And I will most gladly spend and be utterly spent for your lives. If I love you more, am I loved less?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But granted, I did not weigh you down; yet, crafty fellow that I am, I took you in by deceit.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Surely I did not take advantage of you through any of those I have sent to you?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I urged Titus to go, and I sent the brother with him. Titus did not take advantage of you, did he? Did we not walk in the same spirit? Not in the same footsteps?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Have you been thinking all this time that we are defending ourselves to you? It is before God, in Christ, that we speak; and all of it, beloved, is for building you up.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For I am afraid that somehow when I come I may find you not as I wish, and that I may be found by you not as you wish; that somehow there may be strife, jealousy, outbursts of anger, selfish rivalries, slander, gossip, arrogance and disorder.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I am afraid that when I come again my God may humble me before you, and I may mourn over many of those who sinned earlier and have not turned back from the impurity, sexual immorality and debauchery that they practised.

notes.note: Almost all interpreters agree that Paul is describing his own experience in the third person; verse 7 makes this plain when the revelations turn out to be his. The indirection lets him report the vision without making it a boast about himself. Fourteen years before this letter would fall in the early 40s, a period of his life about which little else is known.

The verb means to seize or carry off suddenly and by force; it is used of robbers and of wild animals as well as of being taken to heaven. “Caught up” is the usual rendering and is not wrong, but “snatched away” keeps the abruptness and the sense that the man did nothing to bring it about. The same word and rendering recur in verse 4.

Jewish writings of the period speak of several heavens stacked one above another, sometimes three and sometimes seven. Most scholars think Paul means the highest, and that “paradise” in verse 4 names the same place rather than a further stage. “Paradise” was the Septuagint’s word for the garden of Eden and had come to mean the blessed place in God’s presence.

notes.phrase: even given the extraordinary character of the revelations
notes.traditional: And lest I should be exalted above measure through the abundance of the revelations
notes.note: The edition translated here attaches this phrase to the end of the sentence in verse 6 and begins a new sentence with “Therefore”. Some manuscripts lack “therefore”, and many translations then join the phrase to what follows: “And because of the extraordinary revelations, to keep me from becoming conceited, a thorn was given me.” The grammar is rough on either reading and the connection is disputed.

The Greek word can mean a pointed stake, but in the Septuagint and everyday usage of the period it usually means a thorn or splinter. What Paul refers to is unknown: a chronic illness or bodily affliction is the commonest suggestion, and persistent opponents or persecution is another. The phrase “messenger of Satan” could equally be translated “angel of Satan”, since the Greek word covers both.

The verb means to finish, accomplish or bring to its goal. “Made perfect” is the traditional rendering, but “perfect” now suggests flawlessness, whereas the point is that power reaches its full effect where there is weakness. Most translations keep “made perfect”.

This rare verb means to take up quarters or come to dwell in or over a place. Many scholars hear an echo of the Septuagint’s language for God’s presence dwelling in the tabernacle, though that is not certain. “Rest upon” is the usual English rendering and loses the image of taking up residence.

The adjective is from the same word family as “power” in verse 9, and Paul is completing that thought: Christ’s power dwells on him in his weakness. “Then I am strong” is the familiar rendering and is equally accurate as English; “powerful” is used here so that the link with verse 9 can be heard.

The phrase combines “apostles” with an adverb meaning “exceedingly, beyond measure”. Most scholars take it as Paul’s sarcastic label for the rival missionaries who had come to Corinth; a minority think he means the leading apostles in Jerusalem, in which case the tone is not mocking. The same phrase occurs in 11:5.

The Greek word was the ordinary term for a civic gathering and the Septuagint’s word for Israel assembled before God. “Church” is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. This translation uses “assembly” throughout so that the one Greek word is recognisable everywhere.

The Greek word means a person’s life or self, and “for your lives” here amounts to “for you”, as several modern translations render it. “Souls” is the older rendering, but it suggests to a modern reader an immaterial part of the person as distinct from the body, which is not the point here.

notes.phrase: crafty fellow that I am, I took you in by deceit
notes.traditional: being crafty, I caught you with guile
notes.note: Paul is not confessing; he is voicing, with irony, a charge made against him. The suspicion seems to have been that although he took no support for himself, he was getting at the Corinthians’ money indirectly through his associates and the collection for Jerusalem. Verses 17 and 18 answer that charge.

The word “again” can be taken with the coming, as here, or with the humbling: “that when I come my God may again humble me before you.” The second reading would allude to an earlier painful visit (compare 2:1). The word order allows either and scholars are divided.

The traditional rendering is “repented”, which most translations keep as an established term. In current English “repent” centres on feeling sorry, whereas the Greek word, shaped by the prophets’ call to return to God, means a change of direction in mind and conduct. This translation uses “turn back” throughout.

candidates.reason: Ranges from the physical body to human nature opposed to God, and translations vary widely (flesh, body, sinful nature); readers need to know when it is the same word.
Rendered “soul”, “life” or “self” across translations, and “soul” imports a body–soul dualism the word usually lacks; needs one policy.
Recurs in vice lists and in the Gospels’ divorce sayings, with renderings ranging from “fornication” to “sexual immorality” to “prostitution”.
A key Pauline word rendered “boast”, “glory”, “rejoice” or “take pride” in different places; the thread through Romans and the Corinthian letters is lost if it varies.
Covers pleading, urging, encouraging and comforting; a register entry should fix which English word goes with which sense.
